ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: The pancreas has exocrine and endocrine functions; disorders range from acute pancreatitis to pancreatic cancer. Clinical reasoning links presentation, labs, imaging, and severity to guide urgent care and long‑term management.

sections.p: Pancreatic disorders include acute/chronic pancreatitis, pancreatic necrosis, pseudocyst, and neoplasms. Diagnosis requires clinical suspicion, enzyme elevation, and imaging.
b: Acute pancreatitis: ≥2 of abdominal pain, serum amylase/lipase >3× ULN, imaging findings.
Chronic pancreatitis: persistent pain, calcifications, exocrine insufficiency, or ductal changes on imaging.

sections.p: Acute pancreatitis severity is graded by the Revised Atlanta Classification (mild, moderately severe, severe) based on organ failure and local complications.
b: Mild: no organ failure, no local complications.
Moderately severe: transient organ failure (<48 h) or peripancreatic fluid collection.
Severe: persistent organ failure (>48 h).

sections.p: Identify the precipitant to target therapy; common causes differ by setting.
b: Gallstones – most common worldwide.
Alcohol excess – frequent in adults.
Hypertriglyceridaemia >1000 mg/dL.
Trauma, ERCP, infections (e.g., mumps, HIV, TB).
Medications (azathioprine, valproate).
Herbal or traditional remedies causing toxin‑induced injury.

sections.p: Typical acute pancreatitis presents with sudden epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, and vomiting; chronic disease shows recurrent pain and steatorrhea.
b: Pain worsens after meals, improves leaning forward.
Weight loss, oily stools, diabetes onset in chronic disease.

sections.p: Select tests that answer specific clinical questions; adapt when resources are limited.

t.b: Is there pancreatic enzyme leakage? >3× ULN supports acute pancreatitis; normal does not exclude it.
Is gallstone disease present? Detects stones, biliary dilation; if unavailable, use bedside FAST for fluid.
What is the extent of necrosis or fluid collection? Guides severity and need for intervention.
Is hypertriglyceridaemia the trigger? Levels >1000 mg/dL suggest causality.
Is endocrine function impaired? Detects new‑onset diabetes in chronic disease.

sections.p: Recognise signs that indicate life‑threatening progression.
b: Persistent organ failure (respiratory, renal, cardiovascular).
Infected pancreatic necrosis (fever, leukocytosis, worsening pain).
Hemorrhagic pancreatitis (drop in hemoglobin, hypotension).
Pancreatic pseudocyst rupture.

sections.p: Treat the cause, provide supportive care, and monitor for complications.
b: Fluid resuscitation with isotonic crystalloids (goal: maintain MAP > 65 mmHg).
Analgesia: opioids preferred for severe pain; avoid NSAIDs if renal risk.
Nutritional support: early oral feeding if tolerated, otherwise enteral tube.
Treat underlying cause: cholecystectomy for gallstone pancreatitis, alcohol cessation, triglyceride‑lowering measures.
Antibiotics only for proven infection or prophylaxis before invasive drainage.

sections.p: Long‑term care reduces recurrence and complications.
b: Educate on alcohol avoidance, low‑fat diet, and weight control.
Vaccinate against hepatitis B and pneumococcus in chronic disease.
Screen for diabetes annually.
Imaging surveillance for pancreatic cystic lesions if present.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic pancreatic pain or enzyme elevation.
b: Peptic ulcer disease.
Biliary colic/cholangitis.
Mesenteric ischemia.
Gastric volvulus.

sections.p: Beware of false‑negative or misleading findings.
b: Serum lipase may be normal in very early or late presentation.
Ultrasound may miss small stones in the common bile duct.
CT can underestimate necrosis if done too early.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe abdominal pain with vomiting and hypotension.
Persistent fever, increasing abdominal distension, or confusion.
New onset jaundice with abdominal pain.

faq.q: Why can lipase be normal in early pancreatitis?
faq.a: Enzyme release may not have peaked yet; repeat testing after 6–12 h improves sensitivity.

faq.q: When is surgery indicated in acute pancreatitis?
faq.a: For infected necrosis not responding to antibiotics or for biliary obstruction not amenable to endoscopic removal.

faq.q: How does chronic pancreatitis cause diabetes?
faq.a: Destruction of β‑cells reduces insulin secretion, leading to pancreatogenic (type 3c) diabetes.

exam: Describe the Revised Atlanta Classification and its clinical implications.
List the three most common causes of acute pancreatitis worldwide and explain how you would investigate each.
Explain the rationale for fluid resuscitation targets in severe pancreatitis.
